newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Army says half of Colombia's mayors back rebels.
newsitem.headline: Army says half of Colombia's mayors back rebels.

text.p: Colombia's leftist guerrillas have the direct or passive support of more than half the country's mayors, according to excerpts from a confidential army report published by Semana magazine on Sunday.

Guerrilla influence was strongest in the oil-rich northeastern provinces of Casanare and Arauca and neighbouring Norte de Santander and Santander, the respected political magazine said, citing the military document.

Of a nationwide total of 1,059 mayors, 138, or 13.1 percent, have direct links with the three main rebel armies. The army classes another 462, or 44 percent, of the nation's mayors as coming "under the influence of terrorists."

"Information tends to show that many mayors attend clandestine meetings in which they collaborate to promote the political aims of the guerrillas ... they hide the rebels from the authorities and divert part of their municipal budget toward swelling these criminals' coffers," Semana quoted an unnamed military source as saying.
One Western defence attache recently told Reuters that he estimated more than 40 percent of Colombia was under the de facto economic and political control of the rebels.

The government estimates the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), set up as a pro-Soviet force 1964, the Cuban- inspired National Liberation Army (ELN), founded in the mid-1960s by radical Roman Catholic priests, and the Maoist People's Liberation Army (EPL) muster a combined force of about 12,000 fighters.
Independent analysts, however, said the country's guerrilla armies number at least 18,000 men and women.

The army report regarding the level of guerrilla support among local government officials comes against the backdrop of rising concerns about law and order in the lead-up to mayoral elections in October.

Guerrilla groups and right-wing paramilitary gangs, the sworn enemies of the rebels and their leftist sympathisers, have warned they will not allow any candidates to campaign in their territories if they are seen as a potential threat to the status quo.
The army frequently condemns the legalised Communist Party and the Patriotic Union -- a movement that grew out of a failed peace process in the mid-1980s -- as being the guerrillas' political wing.
